Charania went on "NBA Today" Friday after breaking the news to flesh it out more: "In the last several days, I'm told, Murray has met with the organization, has made it clear to them that he wants to go somewhere else and play a meaningful, key role on another team," Charania said on the program . "And we've seen Dejounte Murray, especially on social media, express his frustration with how things are going there. Clearly, it is not working out there. He is not going to be playing basketball in New Orleans for the time moving forward here." Charania noted that in Murray's absence, the Pelicans will turn over the lead guard position to 2025 No. 7 overall pick Jeremiah Fears. The 20-year-old Oklahoma product has averaged 18 points and nine assists in the three games Murray has missed this season. Murray's been available for only 54 Pelicans games since he came aboard ahead of the 2024-25 campaign. He suffered a torn Achilles that season , and that injury kept him out of a good portion of last season, too . Murray's best NBA season occurred in 2021-22, when he earned his All-Star recognition and led the league in steals during his final go-around with the San Antonio Spurs. stories.title: LaMelo Ball sure looks like the difference: Timberwolves and Hornets trending in opposite directions after trade
stories.summary: Minnesota is making moves in the West with LaMelo Ball, while Charlotte is stumbling in the East without him.
stories.detailText: We will stipulate that, when it comes to success and struggle in the NBA, the answer is never just one thing. There's plenty that goes into teams' fortunes rising and falling, and all sorts of stuff can factor into the difference between living in the penthouse and taking up residence in the outhouse. With that caveat in place: While the Minnesota Timberwolves were doing this in Minneapolis on Thursday, en route to dismantling the Dallas Mavericks, 133-94 … … and the Charlotte Hornets were doing this in Phoenix on the same night, en route to a desultory 101-96 defeat … … it was hard not to note the Just One Thing that seems to be contributing to the difference between Minnesota and Charlotte. Or, rather, the Guy Wearing No. 1. After walloping a pretty good Mavs team, the Wolves are 9-3, in third place in the Western Conference, with the NBA's best net rating . They've won five in a row, and six out of eight since losing superstar No. 1 option Anthony Edwards to knee surgery . They've outscored their opponents by a total of 161 points this season; according to Justin Kubatko of Statitudes , that's the largest point differential through 12 games in Wolves franchise history — by 50 points . After falling in Phoenix, mustering just 96 points against the league's fourth-worst defense , the Hornets are now 4-8, tied for 10th in the East, with the NBA's No. 26 net rating . They've lost seven of eight, have logged more turnovers than assists four times in 12 games , and have already failed to crack 100 points six times — as many times as Charlotte finished south of the century mark all of last season . Again: It's not just that LaMelo Ball used to play for the Hornets, and now he plays for the Wolves. The operating theory for how Charlotte would generate offense in the absence of its one-time linchpin rested largely on continued growth and elevated production from Brandon Miller, Kon Knueppel and the re-signed Coby White, with a dash of second-unit contribution from veteran Dennis Schröder. The Hornets have gotten a grand total of 97 minutes thus far from White, who's on a minutes restriction as he works his way back from a left calf strain, and Knueppel, who'll miss the next several weeks with a balky left hamstring . Schröder's also on the shelf with a hamstring strain ; Miller, the team's leading scorer, has missed the last two games with a groin injury . Any team would struggle to score without the bulk of its perimeter firepower, ball-handling and shot creation. It has to be painful, though, to be mired in such a horrific offensive morass mere months after consciously choosing to bid farewell to Ball, the player whom both the eye test and the advanced numbers suggested served as the rising tide that lifted Charlotte's offense last season. And it must be particularly galling to be suffering through the doldrums while watching LaMelo have exactly the same kind of effusive, elevating effect in the Twin Cities. Ball had nine of the Wolves' 33 assists in the blowout win over the Mavericks on Thursday — Minnesota's fourth 30-assist game of the season , more than anybody but the Hawks, Warriors, Nuggets and Spurs . Those helpers led to 19 Minnesota points, in addition to the 22 that Ball scored himself; for the season, he's directly creating 56.9 points of offense per 100 possessions for the Wolves, according to Databallr , which is 20th in the NBA — and nearly five points-per-100 more than White, who leads this season's Hornets. The Wolves generate a higher share of their shots at the rim when LaMelo's on the floor than when he's off it. Their 3-point shooting goes through the roof in his minutes, and nearly every member of the team sees a bump in shot quality when playing alongside him . The Wolves are more efficient in the half-court when Ball's at the controls, and they get out in transition way more often with him out there. Minnesota's team-wide effective field-goal percentage spikes by 6.5% with LaMelo on the floor — the largest on/off split on the team, and one of the largest among all NBA players to log at least 200 minutes this season, according to Cleaning the Glass . The numbers tell a compelling story. So, too, does the joy that seems to leap off the screen from so many of the Wolves as they run with LaMelo — orbiting, emulating and ultimately benefiting from the irrepressible style and flow with which he plays. "I think when you have a guy like Melo, he makes it fun for everybody," Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch said after Thursday's win, according to Sarah Todd of the Minnesota Star Tribune . "And the guys can trust in the next pass, next play." That trust is tougher to come by these days in Charlotte, where the Hornets enter Friday's action ranked dead last in the NBA in points scored per possession , field-goal percentage , free-throw attempts , assists and turnovers , struggling to consistently string together quality possessions, even against lesser defensive outfits. "How do we stop the bleeding?" White told reporters after a recent loss to the Detroit Pistons. "There's gonna be turnovers. There's gonna be miscommunications on both sides of the ball. How do we not let it continue to derail us from what we're trying to do?" The loss of a superstar of Edwards' magnitude would've derailed plenty of teams. The Wolves, though, have continued to thrive, buoyed in part by the NBA's No. 1 defense — a unit on which Ball has somewhat surprisingly emerged as a physical and positive contributor at the point of attack. All told, Minnesota has outscored opponents by a whopping 15.5 points per 100 possessions when Ball has played without Edwards — a loftier net rating than even their regular-season leading mark, and more than good enough to stay afloat in the brutally competitive West while Ant continues to rehab his ailing knee. There are plenty of other factors at play. The Hornets have underperformed their expected shot quality by more than any other team in the NBA thus far, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking; the combination of some regression to the mean and the hopefully healthy return of some key pieces should help bolster their offense. And there's plenty of credit to go around in Minnesota, from Rudy Gobert's perpetually stalwart work on the back line to Finch getting career-best play from the likes of Jonathan Kuminga, Ayo Dosunmu and Bones Hyland to a collective closing kick that has the Wolves ranked second in the NBA in fourth-quarter net rating . "We've definitely [elevated] our play in the fourth quarters on both sides of the ball," Finch said . "Getting key stops, rebounding really well, executing, finding really good shots. And LaMelo's been at the heart of a lot of that on offense." LaMelo's presence has been at the heart of a lot of what's gone well for the Wolves, and his absence, it seems, has been at the heart of a lot of what's haunting the Hornets. It's never just one thing. Sometimes, though, one thing can make one hell of a big difference.

stories.title: Josh Hart knows how sluggish Knicks can speed up their slow start
stories.summary: Josh Hart agreed Friday that the team’s slow pace has negatively impacted himself, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby.
stories.detailText: INDIANAPOLIS — Amid a struggling start for the Knicks wings, Josh Hart revealed he’s dealt with injuries since pre-training camp and agreed Friday that the team’s slow pace has negatively impacted himself, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby. All three entered Friday’s game against the Pacers shooting under 40 percent, while the Knicks were dead last in the league in pace at 95 possessions per game. “There’s less chances at the rim,” Hart said. “I think it also affects Mikal and OG. … [Coach Mike Brown] says Mikal is the best runner in the league. So if you have the best runner in the league and you’re not running, you’re wasting one of his talents. If we play faster, we’ll be able to do that. Sometimes OG has smaller guards defending him, so if we run he can be able to seal at the rim, be able to get easy points at the rim, which also can help our rim finishing.” Hart said the solution is to simply push the ball up quicker in possessions, even if that means Jalen Brunson isn’t bringing up the ball. The Knicks were third in the NBA in frequency of field goals in the final four seconds of the shot clock, a stat indicative of a slowly evolving offense. They were also shooting an NBA-worst 57.2 percent in the paint, which is a symptom of few breakaways. The Knicks were 23rd in the league in fastbreak points. “We gotta get the ball out and sometimes that might have to be [Brunson] just running and not going to the ball after a make or a defensive rebound,” Hart said. “Just trying to get a better and quicker flow so it’s not so stagnant in the halfcourt.” Knicks guard Jalen Brunson #11 runs down court after scoring against the Bulls. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post The Knicks made up for some of their poor offense with offensive rebounding and second-chance points . Karl-Anthony Towns overall had a monster opening 10 games for New York. Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell #45 drives to the basket as New York Knicks guard Josh Hart #3 gives chase. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post But Hart, Anunoby and especially Bridges weren’t producing to their standard . Hart has been hindered by physical ailments. He planted his foot wrong in training camp and suffered an ankle injury, which caused him to miss consecutive games last week. On Friday, Hart said he was sidelined for three weeks in September because “I tweaked my calf.” It set back his conditioning and led to limitations in training camp , which Hart explained as a contributor to the clunky start. “This year was a little different. Obviously, a shorter break in terms of the summer [because of the long playoff run] but also I wasn’t physically able to really push my body towards the end of the summer to be prepared for the season,” Hart said. “I had [the calf] injury in September, which kept me out for about three weeks, so I wasn’t able to get in some of that conditioning and some of those legs under me, which is normally the time to do it. “And then, the ankle injury in training camp. So, the ramp up was a little bit slower than I kinda wanted it to be or kinda liked it to be, so I think that’s the biggest thing is just getting my legs under me.” Hart entered Friday shooting just 31.7 percent on 3-pointers — which is well below his average of 41.3 percent from last season. “The shots I’m shooting, I like them. I think that was kinda evident with Cleveland. One of the things: All three of my 3s was just hella short. It was just, those legs, get those legs under me,” Hart said. “Also, on top of that, missing a week in the season, it’s cumulative of six, seven weeks of just not much activity basketball-wise. So, I think that’s just what it is. So, as the season progresses and I’m out there running more, doing all those kinds of things, the performance will follow.”

stories.title: Grading the Mavericks: Cooper Flagg is awesome, and he is only going to get better
stories.summary: He still has bad nights, but the good ones give us hope for something really special
stories.detailText: The Mavericks went 3-1 over the last week and sit at 7-5 overall. They won three in a row at home against Utah ( 112-100 ), Brooklyn ( 130-93 ), and Indiana ( 125-122 ). Minnesota pummeled them to start off their road trip, 133-94 . Cooper Flagg led the team in scoring with 25.3 points per game. Grade: A- The Mavericks, once again, had a three-game win streak spoiled by an embarrassing loss. The Timberwolves are much better than the Kings, but the effort from Dallas was similar. Minnesota got any shot they wanted, exposed the Mavericks’ size and lack of point-of-attack defenders, and effectively ended the game in the second quarter. The three games prior, however, were great. The Mavericks took care of business against two bad teams and beat an Indiana team that always gives them problems. Morez Johnson Jr. has been awesome in his minutes; his early-season coup de grace was a 13-point, 17-rebound (10 offensive) performance against Utah, where he truly looked like the ninth pick for the first time. He said after the game that he was “back” , implying that the injury that hindered him to start the year had dissipated. Caleb Martin has been good in his role as defensive connector. P.J. Washington’s jump shot looks so much better this season, likely because he is using his legs more. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving’s chemistry continues to develop as Irving gets healthier. Speaking of which, Irving played his first back-to-back of the season against Brooklyn and Indiana. Zaccharie Risacher has had his minutes go up and down, mostly correlated to how he is playing game to game. Naji Marshall is one piece that still has not felt right on this team, and his trade status will need to be monitored going forward. The Mavericks have to wash the stink of the Timberwolves loss as they head to Cleveland and Boston on a Saturday/Sunday back-to-back, and then back home for Golden State on Wednesday. Straight A’s: Cooper Flagg Let’s ignore Flagg’s stinker against Minnesota for a second. In the three-game win streak prior, he averaged 29.7 points, 8.3 rebounds, 8.3 assists, shot seven-of-15 from three, and had nine stocks (steals plus blocks). This included a 43-point, 10-rebound game, which brings his 40-point game total as a teenager to five, the most all-time. He also sits only behind LeBron James in 25-point, 5-rebound, 5-assist games as a teenager (Flagg 17, James 22), with 13 games scheduled plus the NBA Cup before his 20th birthday, He is awesome. He is a joy to watch, a fierce competitor, and improves (almost) every game. When his three-point shot is on, as it was over the last four games, he is truly unguardable at age 19. Of course, the preface to this section was ignoring his poor performance in Minnesota. He still has weird off-nights. But he is not even 20 years old, and those should phase out as he grows. One thing has been clear in 12 games so far: a team Cooper Flagg will not be able to lose very often. Failed the assignment: Daniel Gafford Gafford has largely been good this year. He has been healthy, which is key, and he certainly is a lob threat on offense. But his weaknesses, particularly on defense, have been exposed recently. He cannot move in space effectively, which forces him to play drop coverage on pick-and-rolls. This means he drops back in the paint to guard the screener, which inherently leaves space for the ball handler to shoot or pass. Teams have been exploiting this, and it even got him benched against the Jazz. His shot-blocking and big dunks are cool to watch, don’t get me wrong. But Gafford has a bit of the “Boban Syndrome”, where he is really good in short spurts and really bad when he plays extended periods. His minutes in the last four games are already down to just 18.3 a game, eclipsed by Morez Johnson Jr.’s 18.8. With Gafford, less is more. Unfortunately, this means they need their rookie undersized center, who is fresh off shin splints, will need to play more. Dallas may survive, but against bigger teams like the Timberwolves, they’re going to struggle mightily. Extra Credit: Walter Clayton Jr. Clayton Jr. has been one of the more underrated signings in the entirety of the NBA this season. His stats do not jump off the page (7.0 points, 3.0 rebounds, 3.5 assists per game), but when you watch him play, he looks like he belongs. This Dallas roster was in dire need of guard play, and Clayton Jr., last year’s 18th overall pick, has given them great minutes at the one. His assists come with just 1.6 turnovers per game, and he is shooting 37.1 percent from three. His hands on defense are active, which really stands out because he gets a lot of deflections. He is under control handling the ball, and already has the trust of the coaching staff to finish games. Normally, individual plus/minus is a flawed stat because there are four other guys on the court. However, Clayton Jr.’s +43 when he is on the floor this season backs up the eye test. He looks like an NBA point guard, and if he can keep this up, this would be Masai Ujiri’s crown jewel early in his tenure.

stories.title: He’s here, he’s there, he’s every-f—ing-where, VJ Edgecombe
stories.summary: VJ Edgecombe continues to do “VJ stuff” to impact winning for the Sixers.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PA - NOVEMBER 12: VJ Edgecombe #77 of the Philadelphia 76ers dunks the ball during the game against the Toronto Raptors on November 12, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Ted Lasso became an iconic show in short order. The Jason Sudeikis-led comedy series about an American football coach who becomes a football (soccer) coach became a cultural phenomenon. One of the most popular characters is Roy Kent, the grizzled old veteran of A.F.C. Richmond. Kent, portrayed by writer and comedian Brett Goldstein, was once a star of the Premier League, but he’s on his last legs when we meet him in the show. Fans of Kent made up a song at his peak, one they serenaded him with as he gets hurt and leaves the pitch for the final time. He’s here, he’s there, he’s every-fucking-where, Roy Kent , Roy Kent Though he’s only in his second year — and is the polar opposite of “grizzled” — VJ Edgecombe has embodied that song in his young NBA career. There was no clearer example of that than his performance in the Sixers’ 123-112 win over the Toronto Raptors Thursday night. With LeBron James out of the lineup, Edgecombe stepped into a bigger role and looked comfortable in it. “I’m blessed to have a group of guys around me that’s encouraging,” Edgecombe said postgame. “They help me with confidence.” Edgecombe scored 15 points with multiple dazzling finishes at the rim, a couple serious dunks (and then teasing the possibility of doing the dunk contest postgame) and a three. He drove to the rim and made the right reads all night, finding his teammates for eight assists. He continued to crash the glass at a high level for a guard, pulling down eight rebounds. He also continued to defend at a high level, recording three steals and a block. All of this and the general winning plays he makes on a nightly basis have become what’s expected of him. “I just tell him to go do that VJ stuff,” Tyrese Maxey said. “Literally, that’s exactly what I tell him. I say, ‘Hey, man, go do that VJ stuff that you do,’ and he literally goes out there and does VJ stuff. He had 15, eight and eight tonight. Who knows? Next game it may be 20, four and four. He just does VJ stuff. He gets us loose balls. He makes winning plays. He defends. He scores. He does it all.” So much of the noise this offseason surrounding the super team of James, Maxey, Joel Embiid and Jaylen Brown the Sixers have built was about Edgecombe. How would he handle his role changing? Would a drop in usage affect his development? Would the glut of stars hurt Edgecombe’s chances to put up numbers and earn his eventual rookie max extension? Nights like Thursday show why those queries were silly. “When I’m on the floor with those four other guys, it’s kind of in a way where it’s helpful for me,” Edgecombe said, “because I’m in different positions and I’m in a year two — I’m seeing basketball from different standpoints. Some nights two of them might be out. Some nights one might be out. Some nights none might be out. And to be able to just balance the different lineups and just trying to stay consistent throughout it all. “I just want to shout out my teammates for that. They just helped me a lot, especially ‘Rese and Joel. They always just tell me keep going, keep going.” Anyone who watched Edgecombe as a rookie and heard him talk knew he’d excel with this star-studded group. Last season, Edgecombe’s usage was unexpectedly high because the Sixers needed it to be. This season, they’ve needed Edgecombe to flash more of his overall game. And 13 games in, that’s exactly what he’s done. But when guys are out of the lineup, Edgecombe knows his team needs more. “I think this is like the second time he’s done this as well when we’re down somebody that he just comes out a little bit more lively and assertive,” Nick Nurse said. “And I thought … he made some really decisive moves in the open floor — not necessarily break situations, but the flow is still going, and he’s punching through. “And again, I thought he kicked out a few of those, and even on some of the half-court sets, he just attacked aggressively to the paint, and that’s where some of those assists were coming from. So, I just thought he did come with an extra pop, and he’s done that a couple times now this year.“ When Edgecombe was coming out of Baylor, there were comparisons to old friend Jimmy Butler. This writer didn’t see it at the time, but now it makes sense. Some players simply impact winning. They affect the game in every facet. They stuff the stat sheet, but their imprint on the game goes far beyond it. He’s here, he’s there, he’s every-fucking-where. VJ, Edgecombe “I’m just blessed to be in this position,” Edgecombe said, “and at the end of the day, I just want to keep getting better. Some opportunities might not be there, but I think I’m getting better mentally, and that’s the most important part of the game. Sometimes you got to be mentally strong.”

Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Joe Boatman/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Luka Dončić continued his excellent play against the Atlanta Hawks Monday night, when he logged 32 points (11-of-22 shooting), 10 assists, eight rebounds, five steals and two blocks in a 124-114 victory. For much of the game, his primary defender was Dyson Daniels, who led the league in steals in 2024-25 and has earned All-Defensive Team nods the past two seasons. Daniels and Atlanta implemented a variety of schemes to try and slow the Dončić-led Lakers offense but nothing really worked. Los Angeles scored 124 points and posted a 120.4 offensive rating, despite Dončić‘s co-star at guard, Austin Reaves, sitting out the second leg of the back-to-back. After the game, Daniels bestowed quite the complimentary label upon Dončić to succinctly summarize the Slovenian’s offensive dominance. “He’s probably the hardest guy to guard in the NBA right now,” Daniels told reporters. “And then, he’s also a willing passer, so.” Asked Dyson how other guys hitting shots for the Lakers affected how they tried to defend Luka + what happened late in the fourth after cutting their deficit to four: pic.twitter.com/IapXfbTCIf — Malik Brown (@_MalikATL) November 10, 2026 While Dončić flourished individually, his gravity and wondrous playmaking helped role players like Sandro Mamukelashvili (23 points, 7-of-13 shooting), Walker Kessler (21 points, 8-of-12 shooting), Collin Sexton (18 points, 6-of-11 shooting) and Ziaire Williams (12 points, 5-of-10 shooting) produce efficient scoring nights alongside him in Atlanta, which Daniels acknowledged, too. Dončić and the 11-2, West-leading Lakers have been a buzzsaw offensively this season. Generating 122.5 points per 100 possessions, they own the NBA’s top-ranked offense, per Cleaning the Glass. Dončić himself is averaging a preposterous 38.6 points and 7.6 assists per game while shooting 58.7% inside the arc and a career-high 40.8% from deep. He’s taking a league-high 13.4 triples each night and making a league-high 5.5 of them. The Lakers are scoring 131.0 points per 100 possessions when he’s on the court. Dončić may be the engine but his backcourt buddy, Reaves, is crucial to Los Angeles’ success and also off to a ripping start. He’s averaging 24.7 points and 4.7 assists on a .513/.409/.915 shooting split. stories.title: Jalen Green’s fit alongside Devin Booker remains a major concern in Phoenix
stories.summary: The Suns actively pursued Jalen Green, but his early-season struggles have forced uncomfortable questions about his role.
stories.detailText: Suns guard Jalen Green (4) reacts late against the Bucks during a game at the Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix on March 21, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co How much data do you need before you’re compelled to make a decision? In the NBA, the answer to that question is as unique as the front offices tasked with making those decisions. There are countless philosophies surrounding what constitutes meaningful data, how much weight to place on sample sizes, and when statistical trends are reliable enough to warrant action. But here we are, 11 games into the new season, and I know I’m not the only person with two functioning eyes beginning to question whether the Jalen Green experiment is going to work in Phoenix. I’ll admit that I initially viewed Green’s acquisition as more of a necessity than an intentional pursuit. The Suns knew they needed to move Kevin Durant for a multitude of reasons, eventually found a trade partner that was acceptable to him (which is an entirely separate situation worth exploring), and needed to make the salaries work. In my mind, Green was simply part of the financial equation required to facilitate the deal. After all, the Houston Rockets had four seasons of data to evaluate Green. Four years of watching his development, assessing his strengths and weaknesses, and determining whether he was someone they wanted to build around moving forward. Their willingness to include him in the trade suggested that perhaps they’d already reached a conclusion about his long-term value. But apparently, I was wrong. As Sam Amick revealed in his latest piece for The Athletic , Green wasn’t merely a contractual necessity or a convenient piece of salary matching. He was someone the Phoenix Suns actively coveted. “(It) was never gonna get done without Jalen and Dillon (Brooks) in the deal,” Ishbia told me earlier this year. “Those are the two players we wanted. It wasn’t, ‘Hey, how do we fill a salary with these numbers?’ It was, ‘In order to have Kevin Durant on your team, I want Dillon Brooks to help me with my culture and my identity. I want Jalen Green as a 23-year-old up-and-coming leading scorer.’” Ugh. So we actively signed up for this? Last season was supposed to be the year of evaluation for Green, a player who arrived in Phoenix with an unbelievably clean bill of health, only to appear in 32 games due to lower extremity injuries. So there’s data point number one: 32 games. Of course, there’s only so much you can reasonably take away from that sample, considering Green was essentially joining a race that was already three-quarters of the way finished by the time he got involved. Which brings us to this season, the one in which the Suns would finally have an opportunity to evaluate what they actually have in Jalen Green. And the early returns? Less than optimal would probably be the polite way of putting it. Getting benched for the entire fourth quarter against the Charlotte Hornets, a team Green should theoretically thrive against, might be a more accurate description of where things currently stand. And quite honestly, it was the right decision. The Suns had been cooking, putting together an impressive 38-16 run in the first half and establishing the kind of offensive rhythm that has been painfully difficult to sustain this season. Much of this occurred with Green on the bench. But when Green checked into the game with 6:06 remaining in the second quarter, that momentum came to a screeching halt. Charlotte proceeded to unleash a 31-11 run that extended into the third quarter, completely erasing the progress Phoenix had made. During Green’s stint on the floor, from 6:06 remaining in the second quarter until he was substituted out with 5:26 left in the third, the Suns were outscored by 18 points. And that was the last we saw of Jalen Green. Once again, Phoenix struggled to generate productive minutes with Green on the floor, and I believe that gets to the heart of the problem. It’s becoming increasingly difficult to identify how his presence complements the players around him, particularly when the team appears to function more effectively without him. And for a player the organization actively coveted as a centerpiece of the Kevin Durant trade, that’s a pretty troubling development. No one is questioning Jalen Green’s athleticism. No one is questioning his desire, his attitude, his likability, or his character. By all accounts, he’s a stand-up guy who has reached the highest level of professional basketball largely because of his extraordinary physical gifts. His explosiveness, speed, and ability to create separation are undeniable. But when you reach the NBA, physical gifts can only take you so far. At some point, the difference between being a good player and becoming a great one comes down to your ability to understand the game, recognize situations, make the right decisions, and contribute within the structure of a functioning offense. When you’re the second highest paid player on the roster, earning $36.3 million this season, the Phoenix Suns need you to be great. They need you on the floor in the fourth quarter, positively influencing the outcome of basketball games. They need you making intelligent decisions, creating opportunities for your teammates, and understanding when to attack and when to allow the offense to develop. What they don’t need is someone disrupting the offensive rhythm, launching ill-timed three-point attempts that have little connection to what the team is trying to accomplish, or throwing the basketball directly into the hands of the opposition. Unfortunately, we’ve seen far too much of the latter. Green, who ranks 53rd in salary this season, is ranked 113th in scoring (11.8 points per game), 92nd in assists (3.1 assists), 189th in three-point percentage (27.0%), and 246th in NET +/- (-28.0). The Ringer’s Rob Mahoney recently said on the Bill Simmons podcast that Green has gone “from counterproductive to actively bad this season.” I can’t say I disagree. Perhaps some of these struggles can be attributed to the Suns asking Green to operate in a role he’s never truly occupied before, that of a primary facilitator. It’s a reasonable explanation, considering his development in Houston was largely centered around his ability to score rather than orchestrate an offense. But as the games have progressed, I’m beginning to wonder whether that’s even what Phoenix is asking him to do anymore. His assist percentage currently sits at 17.1%, placing him in the 44th percentile this season. That doesn’t exactly suggest a player being tasked with consistently running the offense. It feels more like the Suns want him to occasionally facilitate, score when opportunities arise, and somehow make everything fit together. Therein lies the problem. Green’s presence continues to look awkward within this offense’s structure. His movements feel disconnected from those around him, his decisions frequently interrupt the flow of possessions, and his inability to consistently operate within the team’s offensive framework has become increasingly detrimental. That’s what makes this entire situation such a quagmire. Green is struggling to operate within the confines of everything happening around him, and much of what we’re witnessing mirrors the problems we saw last season. At the time, we could point to his injuries, the late start, and the lack of continuity as reasonable explanations for his struggles. Those were legitimate factors, and they made it difficult to draw any definitive conclusions. But now? We’re beginning to see some familiar patterns emerge. And the Suns, as they seem to be in almost every avenue concerning their ability to build for the future, find themselves stuck between a rock and a hard place. Green’s trade value isn’t particularly encouraging at the moment. If Phoenix were to explore moving him, the return would likely be underwhelming. Any opposing team willing to absorb his $36.3 million salary would have to believe there’s something worth salvaging, and even with his contract becoming an expiring deal next season, there’s a reasonable chance that team would want draft compensation to make the transaction worthwhile. What exactly are the Suns supposed to offer? They don’t have an abundance of desirable draft assets sitting around, waiting to be attached to another expensive contract in hopes of making a problem disappear. They used those up to get off of the Nurkic deal or to acquire Mark Williams and Miles Bridges. We’ve already watched this organization sacrifice enough of its future trying to correct mistakes from its past. So what do you do? One possibility is moving Green to the bench, and quite honestly, that might be the most sensible solution available. We’ve seen a version of this experiment before. In January 2025, Mike Budenholzer finally came to the realization that pairing Devin Booker with another ball dominant shooting guard in Bradley Beal was creating more problems than it was solving. The overlapping skill sets were limiting the team’s offensive ceiling, and something needed to change. We all remember how that went. Beal wasn’t particularly receptive to the adjustment, and the situation became another chapter in the ongoing dysfunction surrounding that roster. Green, to his credit, appears to have a different attitude toward making adjustments. He’s expressed a willingness to evolve his game, embrace more facilitating responsibilities, and has spent time working with Steve Nash to improve that aspect of his skill set. Everything suggests he wants to fit in, wants to improve, and wants to become the player Phoenix envisioned when it acquired him. I don’t question any of that. But wanting something to work doesn’t necessarily mean it’s going to work. When you’re playing alongside Devin Booker, the fit becomes especially problematic. Booker possesses an extraordinary ability to control an offense, manipulate defenses, and create scoring opportunities for himself and others. Those are his superpowers. The players surrounding him should be enhancing those abilities, creating space for him to operate, and making his job easier. They shouldn’t be obstacles he has to navigate. Perhaps the answer is allowing Green to find his footing with the second unit, where he can operate with greater freedom, develop some confidence, and establish a rhythm without constantly having to figure out how his game intersects with Booker’s. If he begins finding success in that role, maybe the comfort and confidence he develops can eventually carry over into shared minutes with the starters. Of course, that raises another question. Who starts in his place? Collin Gillespie would seem to be the most obvious candidate, given his familiarity with the offense, his ability to play alongside Booker, and the success Phoenix has experienced with him on the floor. But at this point, you could certainly sell me on Jordan Goodwin as well. Goodwin might not be the traditional facilitator you’re looking for, but he brings something this team desperately needs: a player who can positively influence the game on both ends of the floor without requiring the offense to revolve around him. That’s a conversation worth exploring another day. Ultimately, as I sat there watching the fourth quarter against Charlotte, knowing how ineffective Green had been throughout his minutes, I found myself relieved that he wasn’t on the floor. And I don’t particularly enjoy admitting that. Here was a player the Suns actively pursued as part of the Kevin Durant trade, someone they envisioned becoming a significant part of their future, and I was genuinely pleased that he was sitting on the bench during the most important stretch of the game. Instead, Phoenix leaned on a group that looked much more familiar. Much of the lineup resembled the units that helped the Suns win so many games last season, with Luke Kennard occupying the role previously filled by Grayson Allen for much of the stretch. And what happened? The Suns played well. The offense flowed. Players understood their responsibilities, the ball moved with purpose, and Phoenix outscored Charlotte 29-20 in a fourth quarter that was void of his presence. There was a familiarity to it, a sense that the players on the floor understood how to complement one another rather than compete for the same opportunities. And that’s what makes this entire situation so frustrating. The Suns have invested significant money, opportunity, and organizational belief in Jalen Green. They want him to succeed. They need him to succeed. But right now, some of their most effective basketball is being played when he’s watching from the sideline. Eleven games into the season might not be enough data to make a definitive judgment about his future. But it’s certainly enough to start asking some uncomfortable questions.

stories.title: The Lakers’ schedule will give them runway into big early-season tests
stories.summary: The Lakers could have their best start to a season since winning in the bubble.
stories.detailText: MILWAUKEE, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 11: Luka Dončić #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers reacts after an apparent injury against the Milwaukee Bucks in the fourth quarter at Fiserv Forum on November 11, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Lakers are riding a seven-game win streak and not only sit atop the league with an 11-2 record, they were the first team in the league to play 13 games in this early season. What looked like an easy schedule based on strength of opponent was countered by a rigorous slate that included three back-to-backs and multiple stretches of three games in four nights and five games in seven nights. Los Angeles’ schedule wasn’t nearly as easy as people make it out to be, as referenced by the physical toll it’s already taken on many of its most prominent players, including Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves, who each made it out of the first extended road trip of the season battered up . Between the back-to-backs and surplus of games in a short span, the Lakers came out of this early slate with a lot more answers than questions. There were wins against quality teams like Detroit, Atlanta, Portland and Toronto and survival in potential trap games without one of Dončić or Reaves. “The biggest takeaway is that this is a great group of guys who really enjoy playing together and really enjoy playing for each other,” Redick said of their first road trip. “But we got a lot of work to do and we got to keep getting better.” The Lakers withstood everything the schedule makers threw their way. And for that, they’ll be rewarded with a less demanding runway of games that can serve as another ramp-up before some of their biggest tests of the season. Before taking on Phoenix on Sunday, the Lakers are enjoying their first three-day break of the season, which gave the team time to travel back from Milwaukee and actually practice in El Segundo on Friday. The Suns are 5-6 and coming off a much-needed win against Charlotte. Their early season outlook hasn’t been the best, but they’re among the more talented under-.500 teams the Lakers have played so far. Once the Lakers return from Arizona, they have four games at home over seven days against the Hornets (4-8), Utah twice (1-11) and Sacramento (1-10). When you include the Suns, Los Angeles’s opponents up until Thanksgiving have a combined record of 11-35. This is a crucial stretch for the Lakers to string together some more easy early-season wins while ramping up for a gauntlet to end November, a three-game slate against San Antonio, Memphis and Houston. The Spurs are just half a game behind L.A. in the standings, while the Rockets sit 1.5 games behind and the Grizzlies just three games behind. According to ESPN’s Relative Percent Index (RPI), a tool used to calculate a team’s strength of schedule and, in turn, a power ranking based on said schedule, the Lakers rank fifth in RPI. Houston is first, San Antonio is sixth and Memphis is 17th. The RPI also states that the Lakers have had the 15th-toughest schedule thus far. Not only is that three-game stretch to end the month against three of the best teams the Lakers will have played so far, it’s also three games in four nights, on the road, starting the day after Thanksgiving, including a back-to-back in Memphis and Houston. If they take care of business over these next five games as they have so far this season, the Lakers could enter that slate with a staggering 16-2 record for the first time since the 2019-20 championship season and for fifth time in franchise history, according to Stathead . We’re about to see just how serious a team they are. You can follow Connor on Twitter at @cmorenoNBA .

I’m playing in a f****** game,” Butler told The Athletic. “I’m definitely coming down there to play. So good luck to everybody. Y’all ain’t gonna get too many minutes out of me, but I’m definitely going down there. I want to hoop,” he added. NBA commissioner Adam Silver has had a longstanding fascination with European soccer. Establishing an in-season cup competition within the NBA schedule came from soccer leagues having both a regular-season title, won by the team with the most points over the full year, and a separate tournament (or, in some leagues, multiple tournaments) that runs concurrently with the league season. In England, for example, there are the various divisions -- led by the Premier League -- and also the FA Cup competition. But unlike those European leagues, which play their cup competitions outside of their league schedules, the NBA Cup is built in to the regular-season slate. The 30 NBA teams are split into six five-team groups -- three featuring Eastern Conference teams and three comprising Western Conference teams -- with each team then playing one game against the other four in its group. The winner of each group, plus the team with the best record among the non-group winners, advances to the knockout stage of the competition. How will this impact the regular-season schedule and standings? Typically, the NBA sends out a full 82-game schedule in mid-August. Now, the league sends out only 80 games and leaves a gap of roughly a week to fill in later, depending on how the group stage of the NBA Cup plays out. The two teams from the East and West that lose in the quarterfinals will play their 82nd game against each other. Meanwhile, the 22 teams that fail to qualify for the knockout rounds will have their final two games scheduled -- one at home and one on the road against others eliminated in the group stage. The teams that reach the NBA Cup final will actually play 83 games -- though the championship game won't count toward the standings or any statistical markers. The four teams that reach the semifinals will have completed their 82 games and won't need any other games added to their schedule. Any team that makes it to the semifinals will have that game moved later in the schedule to avoid back-to-back games. The NBA made this change in an effort to avoid having empty days on the calendar while attempting to minimize back-to-backs for all teams as much as possible. Where are the semifinals and final being played? In a shift from previous tournaments, the quarterfinals and semifinals will be played at home sites. The Dec. 11 title game, meanwhile, will move from Las Vegas to the storied Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. NBA commissioner Adam Silver previously said the league was searching for "storied college arenas" to play host to the Cup final. (No venue has been announced for 2027.) Why does the NBA Cup include regular-season games? Before its launch, one of the main questions surrounding the in-season tournament was why any team would be incentivized to compete in it. The NBA ensured teams will be motivated by making every game part of the season and, as in-conference matchups, potentially important to playoff tiebreakers. If this had been set up like the cup tournaments in European soccer, there would have been nothing stopping NBA teams from opting out by sitting their top players for extra rest. Which teams make up the groups? To create the groups, the NBA put the 15 teams in each conference into five pots, separated by their finish last season. Pot 1 included the teams that finished in the top three in the regular-season standings, Nos. 4-6 in the standings went into Pot 2, Nos. 7-9 into Pot 3, Nos. 10-12 into Pot 4 and Nos. 13-15 into Pot 5. As a result, the following groups were drawn: East Group A Detroit Pistons Toronto Raptors Orlando Magic Milwaukee Bucks Brooklyn Nets East Group B New York Knicks Cleveland Cavaliers Philadelphia 76ers Miami Heat Indiana Pacers East Group C Boston Celtics Atlanta Hawks Charlotte Hornets Chicago Bulls Washington Wizards West Group A Denver Nuggets Houston Rockets Phoenix Suns Dallas Mavericks Utah Jazz West Group B Oklahoma City Thunder Minnesota Timberwolves LA Clippers New Orleans Pelicans Memphis Grizzlies West Group C San Antonio Spurs Los Angeles Lakers Portland Trail Blazers Golden State Warriors Sacramento Kings Does one group stand out the most from the others? East Group B is a monster. All five teams -- defending NBA Cup and Finals champion New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Miami and Indiana -- are among the favorites to win the conference in 2026-27. The group stage will also feature reunion games for LeBron James , when the 76ers face the Cavs and Heat. And after guard Tyrese Haliburton missed the entire 2025-26 season while rehabbing a torn Achilles, the Pacers will be back among the East elite and hungry to reach the title game in Indianapolis. What do players get for winning? In 2023, the first year the tournament was held, the players on the winning team received $500,000 each and the runners-up got $200,000. The losing players of the semifinals each got $100,000, and those ousted in the quarterfinals got $50,000. Now, in each subsequent year, the prizes will be slightly higher, as a result of negotiated raises year over year to keep pace with increases in the salary cap and basketball-related income as part of the most recent collective bargaining agreement between the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association. Will anyone earn individual honors for their play in NBA Cup games? There will be an MVP award, as well as an all-tournament team. Will this have any impact on the playoffs? Not beyond the games counting in the regular-season standings (and toward tiebreakers). The only playoff impact comes from the wins and losses accrued throughout the tournament. Though there was debate among league insiders about guaranteeing a playoff berth for winning the tournament, ultimately that idea (or any other to further incentivize teams) was not enacted. Why is it called the Emirates NBA Cup? The league struck a sponsorship deal with Emirates, the Dubai-based airline, to sponsor the tournament after its initial run. The NBA said last year that it went with the most basic titles for both the tournament and its trophy -- the "in-season tournament" and "NBA Cup" -- as a way to introduce the concept to fans. However, using such nondescript names had another clear advantage: It gave the league a blank slate in case it sold the naming rights for the tournament and cup to a sponsor and avoided the complications that could arise by naming them after someone (for example, late NBA commissioner David Stern, one possibility that had been floated before the tournament was officially unveiled). Mandatory Credit: Kyle Terada-USA TODAY Sports The Golden State Warriors are facing perhaps their largest challenge of the season tonight: a road game against Victor Wembanyama and the defending Western Conference champion San Antonio Spurs, without Steph Curry. This won’t be easy. Here’s the full injury report for both teams: Warriors Out — Steph Curry (right oblique tear) Curry was injured early in Wednesday’s game against the Houston Rockets, and will be re-evaluated in two weeks . Needless to say, that’s a huge hit for the team, and now begins the quest of trying to tread water with Curry sidelined. Out — Brandon Williams (left hamstring strain) That aforementioned task is a little bit harder because the team is missing one of their top bench scorers in Williams, who was injured during Monday’s victory over the New Orleans Pelicans. Out — Jimmy Butler III (right ACL repair surgery) Out — Moses Moody (left patellar tendon repair surgery) Out — Kristaps Porziņģis (not with team) No news on either of these three, which is probably a good thing at this point. Probable — Charles Bassey (left toe soreness) Bassey has been huge for the Warriors so far this season, especially in the past few games. So it’s a big win that he’s likely good to go for this game. Spurs Out — Tobias Harris (left calf strain) Harris is playing for his sixth team in his 16th NBA season, but has yet to make his season debut after injuring his calf during training camp. Out — Jayden Quaintance (right knee surgery) Quaintance was the Spurs first-round pick in June’s draft, taken 20th overall. Unfortunately, a knee injury has kept him from making his NBA debut, and it will likely be quite a while before he’s cleared. Questionable — Devin Vassell (left adductor tightness) Vassell, as consistent as they get, has been having his typical strong season thus far. But after playing in San Antonio’s first 10 games, he’s missed the last two with injury … and could miss a third. Questionable — De’Aaron Fox (left hip soreness) Wembanyama is the star of the Spurs, but Fox is often still their motor, thanks to his ball-handling, playmaking, and incredible speed. Fox is having another strong season after making the All-Star Game a year ago, and the Warriors will be given quite a gift if he’s unable to play. Enjoy the game, everyone. It tips off at 6:30 p.m. PT.

teamStories.detailText: Nov 11, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; San Antonio Spurs forward Victor Wembanyama (1) looks on during the first half against the Chicago Bulls at United Center. Mandatory Credit: Matt Marton-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Hello All! After a busy summer, I am happy to return to Pounding the Rock with my first article of the 2026-2027 season. Although I won’t be writing my usual graded box score pieces for each game, I am excited to introduce a weekly power rankings series based on the average Four Factor Index (aFFI) that I first wrote about last year (interested readers can get a brief overview of the methodology behind this index here ). As noted last season, the basic idea behind aFFI is that it assesses a team’s average performance during a defined period (e.g., the season to date, the most recent X-game period, etc.) based on the team-opponent differentials it has achieved with respect to Dean Oliver’s Four Factors of Basketball Success: effective field goal percentage (EFG%), turnover percentage (TOV%), offensive rebounding percentage (ORB%), and the ratio of free throws made to field goals attempted (FTM/FGA). Because aFFI focuses on team-opponent differentials , I add a delta symbol in front of each term (i.e., ∆EFG%, ∆TOV%, ∆ORB%, ∆FTM/FGA). In contrast to the highly subjective and vaguely defined “rich tapestry” approach of many sports media pundits (looking at you Nick Wright), the aFFI ranks teams based on purely objective, observable statistics. Furthermore, over the course of a season, the relationship between aFFI and win percentage is exceptionally strong, with variation in the former accounting for just over 95% of variation in the latter in the 2025-2026 season, as shown in Figure 1 below. In short, over a sufficiently long period, a team’s aFFI is highly associated with it’s ability to win games. View Link As powerful a tool as aFFI can be, it is critical to note that the current NBA season remains extremely young, with the average team having only played 12-13 games thus far. As such, we are still firmly in territory where small sample sizes can generate anomalous patterns, sometimes resulting in a striking disconnect between any given team’s aFFI and observed wins. Although this means that we should take these early season rankings with a grain of salt, it does not necessarily mean that the more surprising results are purely statistical artifacts. In fact, some of these findings provide valuable insights about teams that are likely notably better or worse than their current record might suggest. Bearing all of this in mind, Figure 2 below provides the full aFFI power rankings for the 2026-2027 season to date, reflecting all games played through November 12th. View Link How are the Spurs looking so far this season? They currently rank fourth according to aFFI behind Minnesota, Boston, and Houston, although the range of scores between 2nd (Celtics) and 5th (Lakers) place is quite narrow. A deeper dive into the individual factors reveals that San Antonio’s current position stems from them being very good everywhere but not exceptional in one or two key areas that receive an outsized amount of weight in determining aFFI. In particular, the Silver and Black’s average ∆EFG% percentile (55.46) suggests that they’ve typically had a solid but unspectacular edge in shooting efficiency from the field over their opponents. Because the ∆EFG% average percentile receives a nearly 47% weight in calculating each team’s final aFFI, this plays a huge role in diminishing their overall ranking. San Antonio has performed better with respect to the other three factors, especially ∆ORB%, where they enjoy the third highest average percentile of any team in the league. The importance of relative field goal shooting efficiency in driving aFFI is showcased especially well by first-ranked Minnesota, a team that is actually worse that the Spurs according to every average percentile outside of ∆EFG% (including a subpar ∆FTM/FGA average percentile value of just 46.17). However, the Timberwolves have been absolutely crushing their opponents in relative field goal efficiency through a combination of solid offensive efficiency and excellent defense. As a result, their ∆EFG% average percentile is 70.34, over two points higher than the second-ranked team in this area (the Blazers) and almost 15 points higher than San Antonio. Examining the current set of aFFI rankings as a whole, one generally finds that each team’s ranking is highly correlated with its win percentage, as well as common assessments of team quality that exist across the sports media landscape. However, there are some notable exceptions worth discussing, as Figure 3 illustrates below. Chief among these is the Philadelphia 76ers, who currently rank just 15th in aFFI despite enjoying a 10-3 record and significant positive buzz about their status as a championship contender. In a vacuum, this outcome seems to cast doubt on the viability of aFFI; however, there are at least two key issues to consider: Philadelphia’s average ∆EFG% percentile (47.59) is solidly below average, which is extremely ominous in a sport where relative offensive efficiency is an overwhelming determinant of long-run success. This issue shines through across several of the most basic box score statistics. For example, the 76ers’ currently rank 21st in the league in points per game (111.1), have a PPG differential of just +1.8, and have a lower average FG% and eFG% than their opponents. Put simply, although Philly has managed to display an impressive aptitude for winning early in the season, their current statistical profile is much more aligned with that of an average NBA team. As mentioned above, the average team has only played about a dozen games so far this season. Consequently, it’s still too early to talk about aFFI scores as providing a truly rigorous, mature representation of team quality. Once again, the 76ers’ current situation is illustrative, as their schedule to date includes three bad losses and a number of close wins. Without many other games to look at, this small collection of events probably paints a bleaker statistical picture than the team truly deserves. In other words, it wouldn’t surprise me if Philly eventually emerges as a true contender according to aFFI over time, the limited data to date just aren’t consistent with that profile. View Link Given how much basketball remains, I cannot emphasize enough that this first entry in the aFFI power rankings for 2026-2027 should be treated with caution. Even so, the season to date has seen the emergence of a tentative set of front runners, including the surging Silver and Black (who could easily climb into second place with a good performance tonight). I expect that a few teams will rise steadily up the rankings over time, with Philly and Atlanta being especially likely candidates. In any case, I look forward to providing an update next week!

teamStories.summary: Three-point specialist Doug McDermott has retired from the NBA after 12 seasons spent with seven teams.
teamStories.detailText: Doug McDermott announced his retirement Friday after 12 seasons in the NBA. A first-round pick in the 2014 draft, McDermott carved out a career as a 3-point specialist while playing for seven different teams. In 726 career regular-season games, he averaged 8.5 points, but he shot 41% from beyond the arc, most often in a reserve role. McDermott, 34, was drafted 11th overall by the Denver Nuggets , but he was traded to the Chicago Bulls on draft night. He spent his first 2½ seasons in Chicago before becoming a journeyman around the league, which included stints with the Oklahoma City Thunder , New York Knicks , Dallas Mavericks , Indiana Pacers and San Antonio Spurs . He played his last two seasons for the Sacramento Kings from 2024 to 2026, appearing in 71 games during that span. McDermott burst onto the national scene during his college basketball career where he was a three-time All-American at Creighton , where he played for his father, Greg McDermott, and led the school to four straight NCAA tournament appearances from 2010 to 2014. He led the nation in scoring in 2013-14, won national player of the year as a senior in 2014 and finished his career with the fifth-most points in NCAA Division I men's basketball history (currently seventh). Creighton basketball retired his jersey in December 2023. McDermott's agency, Priority Sports, announced his retirement.

How real are the Lakers, Spurs and the 10 teams slugging it out in the West?
teamStories.summary: Breaking down the early-season runs from a loaded Western Conference.
teamStories.detailText: The Western Conference is tough, a slugfest, a large predicament. None of that is new information. There was, however, a stat from last week that stopped me in my tracks. It was the moment where the West's top-five teams were all on winning streaks of at least four games for the first time since conferences began. All of the current top 10 teams in the West have won at least six of their past 10 games. All of the current top-five are on a winning streak. Six of the current top-10 teams have won their last game. The four teams that have lost? It's because they had to play another top Western Conference team. According to the NBA, eight of the top-10 teams in offensive rating are in the West, six of the top-10 teams in defensive rating are in the West, and seven of the top-10 teams in net rating are in the West. It is still early in the process of the regular season. These teams are still learning who they are on this journey. It is also very real that early success can lead to even more buy-in, which can sustain a team over the course of a season. How real are these early-season runs from the Western Conference? Let's take a look at each team. Los Angeles Lakers (11-2) Yes, Luka Dončić is still on a preposterous run to start the season. Yes, Austin Reaves (who suffered a heel injury on Wednesday) is having a career. And, yes, the Lakers currently have the best offense in basketball. What could make this stick, though, is the belief this team has and the effort it's given on defense. There is an activity the Lakers have brought to the defensive end of the floor. It's not particularly new from what they've attempted to do in the past, but the execution appears more consistent throughout the roster. Switching on- and off-ball actions, working to contain drives and showing early help have been hallmarks of the Lakers' defense. Luka Dončić and the Lakers have reason to smile. (AP Photo/Justine Willard) AP Photo/Justine Willard Walker Kessler's impact has been felt with his work to not just protect the rim, but to consistently rotate to get in position. There's a reason he leads the league in total contested shots (150, 11.5 per game). Whether it's from the baseline, elbow or wing, Kessler's timing has been key in the Lakers' ability to protect the paint (opponents average 43.1 points in the paint, fourth-lowest in league). When the Lakers trend smaller with Kessler off the court, the switching becomes more constant and the attempts at activity ramp up, with multiple lineups that can consistently hit those notes. They'll be tested by switching on both ends eventually, but it feels like the vision and the formula are in alignment. San Antonio Spurs (10-2) If there were any questions about the Spurs' ability to rise back to the top of the Western Conference after a wobbly 0-2 start … I believe 10 straight wins provides an answer. The shift to the three-guard lineup of De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper has had its bumpy moments, but appears to be turning a corner. We are starting to feel the moments where a defense is in rotation and all three can attack. That shift also does not take away from the fact the Spurs still can have 48 minutes of quality guard play throughout a game. This opens up lineup versatility (which will be huge come playoff time) and has contributed to the Spurs' overall offensive balance. It also helps that Victor Wembanyama has gotten even better on both ends. In his last five games, he's averaging 36.6 points, 13 rebounds, and 5 blocks in 28.4 minutes a night, while shooting 65.6% from the field and 41.4% from 3. His physicality is showing up in different ways: working to catch in his spots; being in position to set screens lower on the floor; releasing to his rolls quicker. It'll be hard to doubt the Spurs if the execution continues to level up. Minnesota Timberwolves (9-3) Minnesota had shown the formula and potency of its starting lineup to start this season. That the Timberwolves have been able to expand it while Anthony Edwards has been on the shelf speaks volumes. If the question is where exactly would LaMelo Ball elevate the Wolves, the answer has been everywhere. Ball's playmaking has enhanced their transition and pick-and-roll attack. The shotmaking and drives have added another layer. Jonathan Kuminga has continued to showcase the value of being wanted by doing exactly what the Wolves have needed him to do. Jaden McDaniels and Ayo Dosunmu remain aggressive. What boosts this attack is the fact that the strong defense has held up: activity, ball pressure, off-ball stunts to disrupt. Size and length to switch and bother with Rudy Gobert roaming in the paint can cause chaos. It's hard to imagine this team will not continue to build on its emerging confidence and chemistry. Houston Rockets (9-3) It's the combination of a reliable, strong defense and a commitment to evolving their offense that has helped the Rockets ascend to start this season. Their best moments have come when they have gotten the ball up quick, gotten to multiple actions and kept things moving. Kevin Durant is fully scoring within the flow of their offense, meaning you have to defend multiple things and then Kevin Durant gets the ball. Fred VanVleet has steadied the ship, mixing in pull-up 3s while reading defenses to make plays (without turning the ball over). It's not just that all of their young players are able to "slide down a slot" — their roles are more concise, allowing for more consistency and confidence. The challenge is, will they revert to old habits if either the defense or offense slides backward? Portland Trail Blazers (8-3) A hallmark of this Blazers start has been a collective commitment to buying into their roles and working to do the little things every single night. Damian Lillard's return has been riddled of reminders of the talent he brings to the table. The logo 3s are one thing, the ability to mix in a timely drive is another, and he's willing to put the work in on the defensive end. Toumani Camara will attempt to guard everyone in an opposing jersey. The emergence of Sidy Cissoko means the Blazers have a consistency of guard, wing and big play throughout their lineups. It's less about if they can do it, more of a matter of how many times can they repeat it. No matter where they land in the standings, you'll have to deal with the Blazers all year long. Will they be ready for the success that comes with it? Golden State Warriors (8-4) Well, the test for Golden State now is how real can this run be with Stephen Curry out for an extended amount of time? Curry was tremendous to start the season, but the Warriors were combining his excellent play with working to evolve offensively. More pick-and-roll (with more cutting around it), more willingness to attack matchups, mixing in their traditional splits vs. leaning on it as a base. Yaxel Lenderborg has been a revelation, continuing to gain trust with each performance. Now we'll see just how strong that base is and if the defense that has impressed early can hold up in a scenario where they will have to get stops. It's always been about if the Warriors can win enough regular-season games to get the true payoff in the playoffs. Oklahoma City Thunder (8-4) An unfortunate amount of injuries has led to the Thunder having to work through a different kind of adversity early in the season. If there is one thing about this team, it's that it's always believed in internal growth and optionality. The Thunder have always worked to stay consistent with their approach, and that's what may be the thing that helps lift them through this season. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander being moved off-ball can make him more sudden in a universe where teams may throw more attention his way. There's plenty of opportunity for Jared McCain and Ajay Mitchell to make an impact offensively. But can they grind out enough offense over the course of the season? If nothing else this team will have to defend at an elite level, and if the defense sticks, the Thunder will be no fun to deal with. Memphis Grizzlies (7-4) What a contrast of two months as the Grizzlies went 6-0 in October and have gone 1-4 as of this writing in November. And all four of those losses came in the Grindhouse; home losses are the most consistent regret a Western Conference team can have. There's a reason for their early success, though: It's been a team effort on both ends. Cameron Boozer has helped to elevate what they want to get to offensively. Ty Jerome has been game to take, make, decel and stepback his way to victory. There's a sneaky depth to this team that can be felt from game to game. The big thing is seeing how they adjust as more scouting reports and game plans come in. Taking the league by surprise is one thing, but how will they respond once they've earned a level of respect? Denver Nuggets (6-4) This is not the start the Nuggets had in mind, but the building blocks have not disappeared. On the season, Jamal Murray is averaging 26.2 points on 50.9% shooting from the field and 51.3% from 3. Nikola Jokić is still Nikola Jokić despite feelings he has fallen off. Cam Johnson has stayed aggressive, DeMar DeRozan adds a different element. The lineup versatility unlocked by the play of Spencer Jones and Trevon Brazile should pay off down the line. The biggest question is, can they get enough out of their defense and can their offense still deliver the fastball? We know how tough Jokić/Murray/Aaron Gordon can be to defend, but if opponents find a consistent comfort, how much does that change the Nuggets' winning formula? Dallas Mavericks (7-5) Cooper Flagg's start to the season is going to bring him and this Mavericks team into conversations that may not have been expected this soon. The team's build is what has intrigued me. Improving on both ends of the floor is not easy, and Dallas has risen from 27th in offensive rating and 19th in defensive rating last season to 12th in offensive rating and ninth in defensive rating. That is something. Dusty May has built in principles the Mavericks have worked to hit. An offense that enhances what Flagg brings to the table, takes nothing away from Kyrie Irving and also empowers the rest of the roster is a positive. Defensively, they have several lineups that can have a lot of size and switchability, and they tend to be a bend-don't-break type of team at their peak. Drives are hard to come by, shots are contested in the paint, you just have to deal with them. As the season progresses, they will have to navigate learning how to win and finding a way to do what they do well consistently.
